title: Accounting: Reading the Numbers of a Business
description: Read a company's balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement and notes, and judge from them whether the business is healthy, where its cash is going and which figures to distrust.
audience: A capable adult who has never studied accounting. They are comfortable with percentages and ratios, they may own shares or work for a business, and they want to read an annual report for what it shows. Australian companies report under AASB standards, which are IFRS, so the course uses IFRS terms and Australian examples. It does not teach bookkeeping, tax or personal finance, and it does not repeat Economics or Decision Theory.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a balance sheet, an income statement and a cash flow statement and say how each figure in one shows up in the others.
You'll be able to explain, from a company's own reconciliation, why a profitable business can run short of cash.
You'll be able to say when revenue and costs are counted, and which parts of a profit figure rest on estimates.
You'll be able to judge whether a low current ratio, a high gearing figure or a very high return on equity is a warning or a feature of the business.
You'll be able to find what you need in the notes of an Australian annual report and read a policy, an estimate and a going concern note for what they commit the company to.
You'll be able to spot the common warning signs, say what to check next, and say what a price-to-earnings ratio and a free cash flow figure do and do not tell you about value.

lessons.title: Reading a balance sheet
lessons.objective: Read a balance sheet to say what a business owns, what it owes and what is left for its owners, and say what its figures leave out.

concepts.title: Asset
concepts.summary: Something the business owns or controls, such as cash, stock, equipment or a right to use a leased store.

concepts.title: Liability
concepts.summary: Something the business must pay or deliver later: suppliers, loans, leases, unearned revenue and provisions.

concepts.title: Equity
concepts.summary: What is left of the assets after the liabilities are deducted. It is measured at recorded cost and is not a bank balance or a sale price.

concepts.title: Current and non-current
concepts.summary: Current means expected to turn into cash, or to be paid, within the next year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer.

misconceptions: Treating equity as cash the owners could take out. Lovisa holds $46.7 million of cash and reports $78.0 million of equity; they are different kinds of figure.
Treating equity as what the business is worth. Assets are recorded at cost and changes in market value are generally not recorded (Lyryx 4.1), so equity says little about earning power.
Reading 'liability' as 'bank loan'. Most of Woolworths's liabilities are trade payables, provisions and leases.
Reading a balance sheet as a record of the year. It is a picture at one date; the income statement and cash flow statement cover a period.
sequence: Open on Lovisa's balance sheet at 28 June 2026 with the totals hidden. Ask who paid for $696 million of assets: the creditors or the owners?
Name the three groups and the equation, and show equity as the leftover (assets less liabilities).
Split each side into current and non-current with the 12-month rule, and note that items are listed by liquidity.

Read the biggest items for each company. Lovisa has a right-of-use asset of $357 million and lease liabilities of $419 million; Woolworths has lease assets of $8.7 billion and lease liabilities of $11.3 billion. Introduce leases as an asset and a liability together.
Say what the statement leaves out: values at cost, one date only, no sense of future earnings.
Close with the check: assets must equal liabilities plus equity, so any one figure can be found from the other two.
examples: Lovisa at 28 June 2026 ($000s): total assets 696,037, total liabilities 618,076, equity 77,961. Equity is about 11% of assets. Cash is 46,735, so equity is not cash.

Woolworths at 28 June 2026 ($M): total assets 34,065, total liabilities 29,155, net assets 4,910, about 14% of assets. Current assets are 7,691 and current liabilities 13,686; the later lessons come back to that.

lessons.title: Every transaction has two sides
lessons.objective: Read a transaction as two changes that keep the accounting equation in balance, and say which items move and whether profit changes.

concepts.title: Double entry
concepts.summary: Every transaction is recorded as equal and opposite entries, so the accounting equation stays in balance.

concepts.title: Debit and credit
concepts.summary: The left and right sides of an entry. They are not good and bad: a debit increases an asset and a credit increases a liability.

concepts.title: Profit flows into equity
concepts.summary: Profit adds to retained earnings, and retained earnings are part of equity, so an event that changes profit also changes equity.

concepts.title: Provision
concepts.summary: A liability recorded for a cost that has been incurred and will be paid later, such as underpaid wages.

misconceptions: Thinking a debit is bad and a credit is good. A debit to an asset increases it.
Treating borrowed money as income. A loan raises cash and a liability together; profit does not change.
Treating a purchase of equipment as a cost of the year. It swaps cash for an asset; profit falls only as the asset is depreciated.

Thinking cash must move for profit to change. Woolworths recorded an additional $710 million provision in 2026; the cost reached profit when the provision was recorded and the cash goes out as payments are made.
sequence: Start with five events at an invented joinery firm: a bank loan, a machine bought for cash, timber bought on credit, a job done on credit, and the supplier paid. For each, name the two things that change.
Keep a running balance sheet and check the equation after every event.
Ask of each event whether equity changes. Only the job does, by the profit on it.
Move to real entries in Woolworths's notes: contract liabilities (cash in before the revenue is earned) and the $710 million provision (cost recognised before the cash goes).
Close with the habit: any event changes at least two things, and profit changes only when revenue or a cost is recorded.
examples: Invented firm. (1) Borrow 50,000: cash +50,000, loan +50,000. (2) Buy a machine for 30,000 cash: cash -30,000, machine +30,000. (3) Buy 8,000 of timber on credit: timber +8,000, payables +8,000. (4) Do a 20,000 job on credit using 6,000 of timber: receivable +20,000, timber -6,000, profit +14,000. (5) Pay the supplier 8,000: cash -8,000, payables -8,000. End: cash 12,000, receivable 20,000, timber 2,000, machine 30,000 = 64,000 of assets; loan 50,000 plus equity 14,000 = 64,000.

Woolworths 2026: trade payables 6,302, accruals 1,791 and contract liabilities 567 make up 'trade and other payables' of 8,660. The additional $710 million provision for underpaid wages raised a liability and a cost on the day it was recognised; cash goes out later, as payments are made.

lessons.title: Reading an income statement
lessons.objective: Read an income statement from revenue down to profit, say where each layer of profit comes from, and separate a recurring result from a one-off item.

concepts.title: Gross profit
concepts.summary: Revenue less the direct cost of the goods sold. What counts as direct differs between companies.

concepts.title: Operating profit (EBIT)
concepts.summary: Profit before net finance costs and tax. Woolworths calls it EBIT and Lovisa calls it operating profit.

concepts.title: Significant items
concepts.summary: Costs or gains a company sets apart so that trading results can be compared. The label is the company's own, because IFRS allows no 'extraordinary' items.

concepts.title: Earnings per share
concepts.summary: Profit attributable to shareholders divided by the number of shares.

misconceptions: Treating revenue as profit. Woolworths keeps about 1.6 cents of each revenue dollar as profit for the period.
Treating profit as cash. Profit counts events when they happen; the cash flow statement follows the cash.
Ignoring a significant item because the company labelled it. A $710 million underpayment cost is real, though it is not a measure of this year's trading.
Comparing profit growth without checking one-offs. Statutory profit rose 21% at Woolworths and profit before significant items rose 17%.
sequence: Walk down Woolworths's income statement layer by layer: revenue, cost of sales, gross profit, branch and administration costs, other expenses, EBIT, net finance costs, tax, profit.
Put Lovisa's beside it. Note that Lovisa lists depreciation on its own line and that finance costs include lease interest.
Read the significant items table: EBIT of 3,105 before, (698) of items, 2,407 after. Read the note behind the largest one, the $710 million wage provision.
Ask what a fair headline is. Compare statutory and before-significant-items growth, and say what each answers.
Add earnings per share and say why it is used to compare years when the share count changes.
examples: Woolworths 2026 ($M): revenue 71,539; cost of sales 51,970; gross profit 19,569; EBIT 2,407; net finance costs 829; tax 426; profit 1,152 (2025: 953, so up about 21%). Before significant items profit was 1,613 (2025: 1,375), up about 17%.
Lovisa 2026 ($000s): revenue 938,763 (up 17.6%); gross profit 775,333 (up 18.4%); depreciation and amortisation 131,289 (up 20.9%); operating profit 158,222; profit after tax 95,590 (up 10.7%).

lessons.title: Reading a cash flow statement
lessons.objective: Read a cash flow statement as three stories, from operations, investing and financing, and say what they show about how the business pays its way.

concepts.title: Operating cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash from the day-to-day activities of the business: receipts from customers less payments to suppliers, employees, interest and tax (under the layout both companies use).

concepts.title: Investing cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash spent on or received from long-term assets and investments, such as stores, equipment and businesses.

concepts.title: Financing cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash from or to the people who fund the business: borrowing and repaying, lease principal, dividends and share issues.

concepts.title: Lease principal
concepts.summary: The part of each lease payment that repays the lease liability. Both companies report it in financing, so operating cash flow is higher than it would be if rent were an operating cost.

misconceptions: Treating a small rise in cash as a weak year. Lovisa's cash rose $6.5 million while it paid out $88.6 million of dividends.
Thinking operating cash flow is profit. Woolworths made $1,152 million of profit and $4,948 million of operating cash flow.
Missing where the rent went. Under AASB 16 lease principal sits in financing, so two businesses with the same real cost can show different operating cash flow.
Assuming every company classifies interest the same way. IAS 7 lets interest paid sit in operating or financing activities.
sequence: Open on Woolworths's three subtotals: 4,948 in, 2,014 out, 2,701 out, and ask what a business that pays for itself looks like.
Classify the lines into operating, investing and financing, and note what each group is about.
Do the same for Lovisa and compare the pattern: both fund stores and dividends from operating cash.
Find the rent. Show the lease liability movement and where the principal and interest are reported.
Close with three questions for any cash flow statement: does operations cover investing, who got paid in financing, and what is not shown (such as principal on leases) that a reader should add back.
examples: Woolworths 2026 ($M): operating 4,948; investing (2,014), of which payments for property, plant and equipment (2,435); financing (2,701), of which lease principal (1,298) and dividends (1,100). Net increase in cash 233. After property, plant and equipment spending and lease principal, about 1,215 of operating cash flow remains against dividends of 1,100.

Lovisa 2026 ($000s): operating 232,764; investing (58,478); financing (167,741), of which lease principal (89,152) and dividends (88,589). Net increase in cash 6,545. Lease payments of 108,866 split into principal 89,152 (financing) and interest 19,714 (within interest paid, in operating).

lessons.title: Why profit is not cash
lessons.objective: Explain from a company's reconciliation why a profitable business can run short of cash, and name the lines (receivables, stock, payables, depreciation, provisions) that account for the gap.

concepts.title: Accrual accounting
concepts.summary: Revenue is recorded when delivered and expenses when received, whether or not cash has moved.

concepts.title: Reconciliation of profit to operating cash flow
concepts.summary: A table starting at profit and adding or subtracting non-cash items and changes in working capital to reach operating cash flow.

concepts.title: Non-cash expense
concepts.summary: An expense deducted in profit with no cash leaving, such as depreciation. It is added back; it is not a source of cash.

concepts.title: Growth consumes cash
concepts.summary: A firm that sells more on credit and carries more stock must fund the gap between paying for goods and being paid.

misconceptions: Believing profit is cash earned. A sale on credit is profit now and cash later.
Believing a profitable business cannot run out of cash. Growth that is funded by customers' credit and stock can.
Calling depreciation a source of cash. It is added back because it was deducted without cash leaving.

Reading a big provision as cash paid. Woolworths's reconciliation adds back a $652 million increase in provisions, largely the wage provision, and its note says interest accrues 'until payments are made'.
sequence: Open on Woolworths's reconciliation: profit 1,152, operating cash flow 4,948. Ask where $3.8 billion came from.
Go line by line: depreciation and amortisation 2,984, stock (351), trade payables +367, provisions +652, other payables +329, deferred tax (288).
State the rule: a rise in receivables or stock lowers cash against profit, a rise in payables or provisions raises it, and depreciation is added back.
Turn it round with an invented printing business whose sales double on 60-day terms: profit up, cash down.
Name the pattern that the textbook case shows: net income each year, receivables, stock and short-term borrowing rising together, cash falling.
Close with the question to ask of any profit: what turned it into, or kept it from, cash?
examples: Woolworths 2026 ($M): profit 1,152; depreciation and amortisation +2,984; impairment +16; share-based payments +86; inventories (351); trade payables +367; provisions +652; other payables +329; deferred tax (288); the remaining small items net to 1; operating cash flow 4,948. The gap of 3,796 is mostly depreciation (79%).

Invented printer, Harbour Print: profit 48,000; depreciation 12,000; receivables up 100,000 (sales doubled to 600,000 on 60-day terms); stock up 40,000; payables up 25,000. Operating cash flow is 48,000 + 12,000 - 100,000 - 40,000 + 25,000 = -55,000.

lessons.title: When revenue and costs count
lessons.objective: Decide in which period a sale or a cost belongs, and say what sits on the balance sheet when cash and recognition do not coincide.

concepts.title: Revenue recognition
concepts.summary: Revenue is counted when control of the goods or services passes to the customer, in the amount the business expects to be entitled to.

concepts.title: Contract liability
concepts.summary: Cash received for an obligation not yet met, such as gift cards and loyalty points. It becomes revenue as the obligation is met.

concepts.title: Matching
concepts.summary: Costs are put in the same period as the revenue they helped earn.

concepts.title: Revenue that rests on estimates
concepts.summary: Where revenue depends on a measure of progress or a forecast, as with unbilled work in progress, the estimates are what a reader should question.

misconceptions: Believing revenue is counted when cash arrives. Retail customers pay at the till; business customers of Woolworths pay about 24 days later, and revenue is counted at the sale.
Counting revenue when an order is placed or a contract is signed. It is counted when control passes, or as work is done.
Treating money received in advance as revenue. A gift card or a deposit is a liability until the obligation is met.
Treating the revenue figure as a fact. Where it depends on estimates of work done, ASIC's questions to Slater and Gordon show what can go wrong.
sequence: Open on Woolworths's policy: revenue is recognised when control of the goods transfers. Then read its loyalty-points wording and ask what happens to the part of the price allocated to points.
Lay out the five steps of IFRS 15 in order and say what each decides.
Place four invented cases in time: a membership paid in advance, work finished but not yet billed, wages owed at year end, and insurance paid for next year.
Move to revenue that rests on estimates. Read ASIC's release on Slater and Gordon: fee revenue and work in progress, and the testing of estimates against history.
Close on gross and net: Enron reported the full value of trades as revenue where rivals reported only fees.

lessons.title: Estimates inside profit
lessons.objective: Judge how much of a profit figure rests on estimates, and say what changes, and what does not, when a useful life, a cost formula or a write-down changes.

concepts.title: Depreciation
concepts.summary: Spreading the cost of a long-lived asset over its estimated useful life. It is an allocation of cost, not a measure of market value or of cash.

concepts.title: Change in estimate
concepts.summary: A new estimate of life or residual value changes the depreciation from that date on; past charges are not restated.

concepts.title: Lower of cost and net realisable value
concepts.summary: Stock is carried at the lower of what it cost and what it is expected to sell for, less selling costs.

concepts.title: Impairment
concepts.summary: A write-down when an asset's recoverable amount is below its carrying amount. It reduces profit and the asset with no cash leaving.

misconceptions: Treating depreciation as cash set aside or cash spent. It is an allocation.
Treating carrying amount as market value.
Thinking a longer useful life changes cash. It changes profit and the asset's carrying amount only.
Thinking one stock formula is 'true'. When prices move, FIFO and weighted average give different profit from the same purchases and sales.
Treating a write-down as cash lost in the year of the write-down. The cash went when the asset or stock was bought.
sequence: Open on a $20,000 machine with a five-year life and $2,000 residual: $3,600 a year. After two years the owner re-estimates six more years and $5,000 residual. Work out the new charge and ask what happened to cash.
Scale it up: Lovisa's depreciation and amortisation is $131 million against operating profit of $158 million, so a modest change in lives moves profit a lot.
Stock: IAS 2 values stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value, with FIFO or weighted average. Read Woolworths's and Lovisa's notes.
Impairment: read the prior-year Woolworths impairments and Lovisa's store impairments, and show they are added back as non-cash.
Close by sorting what in a profit figure is counted from records and what is judged.
examples: Machine: ($20,000 - $2,000) / 5 = $3,600 a year. After two years the carrying amount is $12,800. New estimates of six years and $5,000 residual give ($12,800 - $5,000) / 6 = $1,300 a year, so profit rises by $2,300 a year and cash does not change.

Lovisa 2026 ($000s): depreciation and amortisation 131,289 against operating profit 158,222 (83%). If depreciation were 10% lower, operating profit would be about 13,000 higher; cash is unchanged. Stock written down to net realisable value 20,999 (2025: 14,929). Store impairments 8,879.

Woolworths 2026 ($M): inventories 4,523 less a 58 provision, weighted average cost, lower of cost and net realisable value; prior-year impairments of BIG W 346, MyDeal 45 and Healthylife 17, all added back in the reconciliation.

lessons.title: Working capital and the cash cycle
lessons.objective: Read current assets and current liabilities as a cycle of cash, stock and credit, and judge whether a low or negative working capital is a warning or part of the business model.

concepts.title: Working capital
concepts.summary: Current assets minus current liabilities. Less than zero is a working capital deficiency, or a net current liability.

concepts.title: Days of inventory, receivable and payable
concepts.summary: How many days of cost of sales, or of sales, the balance represents: stock over cost of sales, receivables over sales, payables over cost of sales, each times 365.

concepts.title: Cash conversion cycle
concepts.summary: Days of stock plus days of receivables less days of payables: how long cash is out before it comes back.

concepts.title: Credit terms
concepts.summary: A receivable period means little until it is set beside the terms the business gives, for example 30 days or the 24 days Woolworths gives business customers.

misconceptions: Believing working capital must be positive. Woolworths reports a net current liability of $5,995 million and says why.
Believing a higher current ratio is always better. Wikipedia notes that a very high ratio can mean current assets are not used efficiently.
Treating a long collection period as a problem without checking terms and the age of the receivables.
Treating supplier credit as free. A negative cycle holds only while suppliers keep supplying on those terms.
sequence: Open on Woolworths's going concern note, which explains its own net current liability. Read its reasons aloud.
Estimate the three day counts from the statements and combine them into the cycle: about 31 days of stock, 2 of receivables and 44 of payables.
Set an invented wholesaler beside it: 120 days of stock, 55 days to collect on 30-day terms, 35 days to pay.
Show the textbook pattern: days of stock and days to collect both rising while supplier terms stay at 60 days, and short-term borrowing filling the gap.
Close with the rule: ask what the cycle looks like and who funds it, before judging the ratio.
examples: Woolworths 2026 ($M): current assets 7,691 against current liabilities 13,686, a net current liability of 5,995. Inventories 4,465 on cost of sales of 51,970 is about 31 days. Trade payables 6,302 is about 44 days. Trade receivables 469 on revenue 71,539 is about 2 days. The cycle is about 31 + 2 - 44 = -11 days.
Invented wholesaler, Dunmore Tiles: 120 days of stock + 55 days of receivables - 35 days of payables = 140 days, which someone must fund.

lessons.title: Liquidity and gearing
lessons.objective: Judge whether a business can meet what it owes by reading the current ratio, gearing and interest cover together, and say what leases and classification can hide.

concepts.title: Current ratio
concepts.summary: Current assets divided by current liabilities. It measures accounting liquidity; acceptable levels vary by industry.

concepts.title: Quick ratio
concepts.summary: A stricter test that leaves out stock, so it counts only cash and near-cash against current liabilities.

concepts.title: Gearing
concepts.summary: Another name for leverage: how much of the funding is borrowed. The debt-to-equity ratio is one measure, and which debts count changes the answer.

concepts.title: Interest cover
concepts.summary: Operating profit divided by finance costs: how far profit could fall before interest could not be paid.

misconceptions: Treating a current ratio above 1 as safe. It depends on what the current assets are and how fast they turn.
Counting only bank borrowings in gearing. Lease liabilities are fixed commitments: Woolworths has $5.2 billion of borrowings and $11.3 billion of lease liabilities.
Treating classification as presentation only. A liability due within a year that is shown as non-current improves the current ratio.
Reading healthy profit as the ability to pay debt. ABC Learning was profitable and went into receivership with $1.8 billion of debt.
sequence: Compute the current ratio and the quick ratio roughly for Woolworths and Lovisa, and set each beside the cycle read in the last lesson.
Build gearing two ways for each: borrowings only, then borrowings plus leases. Show how the picture changes.
Add interest cover for both and say what each says about how much profit could fall.
Show how a ratio can mislead: the Centro finding on short-term debt, and ABC Learning's profit and debt.
Close with the idea that a ratio answers one question: pick the ratio for the question you have.
examples: Woolworths 2026 ($M): current ratio 7,691 / 13,686 = 0.56; quick 0.19 using cash and receivables. Borrowings 5,161 and lease liabilities 11,316 against equity 4,910: about 1.1 times on borrowings alone and 3.4 times with leases. EBIT 2,407 over net finance costs 829 is 2.9 times.

Lovisa 2026 ($000s): current ratio 151,373 / 185,454 = 0.82. Loans 87,000 and lease liabilities 418,995 against equity 77,961: 1.1 times on loans alone and 6.5 times with leases. Operating profit 158,222 over finance costs 24,789 is 6.4 times.

lessons.title: Margins and turnover
lessons.objective: Compare businesses by gross, operating and net margin and by asset turnover, and say what a margin cannot tell you.

concepts.title: Margin
concepts.summary: Profit at some level divided by revenue: gross, operating or net. Each level answers a different question.

concepts.title: Asset turnover
concepts.summary: Revenue divided by total assets: how many dollars of sales each dollar of assets produces.

concepts.title: Return on assets from margin and turnover
concepts.summary: Net margin times asset turnover gives profit over total assets, so a thin margin can pay if the assets turn fast.

concepts.title: Classification of costs
concepts.summary: Which costs sit in cost of sales differs between companies, so gross margins are comparable only after checking.

misconceptions: Thinking a higher margin means a better business. Woolworths earns about 1.6 cents per revenue dollar and still reports a 16.4% return on funds employed.
Comparing gross margins across companies without checking what is in cost of sales. Lovisa puts warehouse and outbound freight in distribution costs, outside gross profit.
Treating one year's margin as the normal one. Woolworths has had significant items in 2025 and 2026.
Mixing margins up. Gross, operating and net margins can move in opposite directions.
sequence: Compute three margins for Woolworths and Lovisa from the statements read in lesson 3.
Put the numbers side by side and ask why the two firms differ so much.
Add turnover and show how margin times turnover gives return on assets.
Look at the classification traps: where freight, depreciation and warehouse costs sit.
Look at the one-off trap: Woolworths's margin before and after significant items, and the fact that items appear in both years.
examples: Woolworths 2026: gross margin 27.4%; EBIT margin 3.4% after significant items and 4.3% before; net margin 1.6% (profit 1,152 on revenue 71,539). Total assets 34,065, so asset turnover is 2.1 times.

Invented: two retailers each earn 5% on assets. One has a 10% net margin and turns assets 0.5 times; the other has a 2% margin and turns assets 2.5 times.

lessons.title: Return on equity and return on capital
lessons.objective: Judge whether a high return on equity reflects a good business or a thin equity base, and use a return on capital to compare businesses fairly.

concepts.title: Return on equity
concepts.summary: Profit divided by average shareholders' equity: profit per dollar of equity.

concepts.title: The DuPont split
concepts.summary: ROE equals net margin times asset turnover times accounting leverage (assets over equity).

concepts.title: Return on capital
concepts.summary: After-tax operating profit divided by average invested capital, where the capital comes from shareholders and from debtholders.

concepts.title: Thin equity
concepts.summary: A small equity base, from heavy borrowing, large payouts or reserves, makes ROE large without making the business better.

misconceptions: Treating a high ROE as proof of a good business. Lovisa's is above 100% and Woolworths's about 24%, and thin equity drives much of the difference.

Forgetting that ROE uses profit after interest and ROIC uses operating profit, so only ROIC is untouched by how much is borrowed.
Treating the 15 to 20% 'good' range as a rule. Wikipedia gives it as general, for comparison within an industry.

lessons.title: Reading the notes
lessons.objective: Find what you need in an annual report beyond the three statements, and read a policy, an estimate and a going concern note for what they commit the company to.

concepts.title: Notes to the statements
concepts.summary: Details that the face of the statements leave out: policies, breakdowns and estimates. They are part of the statements.

concepts.title: Critical accounting estimates
concepts.summary: The judgements the company says have the largest risk of a material change. Woolworths names leases, impairment of non-financial assets and provisions.

concepts.title: Going concern note
concepts.summary: The directors' statement that the business can pay its debts as they fall due, with reasons where the balance sheet looks tight.

concepts.title: Auditor's report
concepts.summary: An independent opinion giving reasonable assurance that the statements are not materially misstated. It is not a guarantee.

misconceptions: Thinking the three statements are the whole story. The detail is in the notes.
Thinking a clean audit means a healthy business. An audit seeks reasonable assurance, not certainty.
Thinking compliance with IFRS means the business is sound. It says how the numbers are prepared.
Reading a balance sheet line by its label. Lovisa's 'trade and other receivables' of $29.7 million holds only $3.2 million owed by customers.
sequence: Open with a map of an Australian annual report: directors' report, the statements, the notes, directors' declaration, auditor's report.
Read the basis of accounting in Woolworths's notes: the Corporations Act and AASB standards, which comply with IFRS.
Read the going concern note and the critical estimates note. Ask what each commits the directors to.
Read two notes that change a balance sheet line: Lovisa's receivables and Woolworths's cash that includes card receivables.
Read what ASIC says directors and auditors should focus on, and set it beside Woolworths's own list.
examples: Woolworths: the financial report complies with Australian Accounting Standards and so with IFRS as issued by the IASB; critical estimates are Note 3.5 Leases, Note 3.9 Impairment of non-financial assets and Note 3.12 Provisions; $695 million of the $1,497 million of cash is receivables from card merchants that will be reclassified as receivables in 2027.
Lovisa: trade and other receivables of 29,682 ($000s) are trade receivables 3,177, deposits 4,397, prepayments 13,953 and other receivables 8,155.

lessons.title: Warning signs
lessons.objective: Recognise the common warning signs in a set of statements and in the notes, and say what to check next without leaping to a verdict.

concepts.title: Quality of earnings
concepts.summary: How closely profit is matched by cash over several years.

concepts.title: Earnings management
concepts.summary: Using judgement in reporting or in structuring transactions to alter reported results.

concepts.title: Warning sign
concepts.summary: A pattern that calls for a question: profit and cash moving apart, receivables outrunning sales, estimates changing, debt reclassified, one-offs that recur.

concepts.title: Allowance for doubtful accounts
concepts.summary: A deduction from receivables for amounts not expected to be collected. It is an estimate, and it seldom matches the final loss.

misconceptions: Treating a warning sign as proof of fraud. Creative accounting can follow the letter of the rules, and some patterns, such as a net current liability at a supermarket, are normal.
Treating the end of a regulator's inquiry as a clean bill. ASIC said it had not approved Slater and Gordon's earlier revenue basis, and the firm wrote down assets afterwards.
Thinking only complex schemes mislead. Misclassifying a debt, or recognising revenue early, uses ordinary accounting.
Believing the auditor will catch it. Directors are primarily responsible for their financial report, and the audit gives reasonable assurance only.
sequence: Start with an invented three-year table of a firm whose profit rises while operating cash falls and receivables far outgrow sales. Ask what to check next.
Name the patterns: profit without cash, receivables outrunning revenue, assets that are never written down, debt reclassified, one-offs that recur, estimates that change.
Read three real Australian cases from the pack: Slater and Gordon (ASIC), Centro (Federal Court finding) and ABC Learning.
Read Enron's gap between reported profit and cash as the extreme case.
End on the method: compare profit with cash over three years, receivables with revenue, then read the notes on policy changes and estimates.
examples: Invented Alder Pty Ltd, years 1 to 3: revenue 100, 130, 170; profit 10, 15, 21; operating cash flow 9, 6, -3; receivables 12, 28, 52. Receivables are about 4.3 times their year 1 level against revenue at 1.7 times. Days of sales in receivables go from about 44 to about 112.

Slater and Gordon: ASIC's inquiries concerned goodwill, fee revenue and work in progress, provisions against debtors and whether work in progress was current; in the half year to 31 December 2015 the firm impaired goodwill, reduced work in progress on adopting AASB 15 and increased provisions.

Centro: in June 2011 the Federal Court found eight executives and directors breached the Corporations Act by signing off financial reports that failed to disclose billions of dollars of short-term debt.

lessons.title: What a business is worth
lessons.objective: Read a price-to-earnings ratio, a free cash flow figure and an enterprise value for what they say about a business, and say why accounting profit alone does not give its value.

concepts.title: Price-to-earnings ratio
concepts.summary: Share price divided by earnings per share: the number of years of current earnings the buyer pays for.

concepts.title: Free cash flow
concepts.summary: Operating cash flow after capital spending. It is the cash that can be paid to lenders and owners without harming operations.

concepts.title: Discounted cash flow
concepts.summary: A value found by estimating future cash flows and discounting them for the time value of money; the terminal value is often a large share.

concepts.title: Enterprise value
concepts.summary: The sum of the claims of all who fund the business, creditors and shareholders, so wider than market capitalisation.

misconceptions: Treating a low P/E as cheap. The ratio says what is paid for current earnings, and growth and risk differ.
Treating equity on the balance sheet as value. Lovisa's equity is about $0.70 a share against a $23.25 price, because assets are at cost and earning power is not recorded.
Treating profit as what owners can take out. Free cash flow after leases is a closer guide.
Treating a DCF value as exact. The terminal value is highly sensitive to the discount rate and growth.
sequence: Open on a real table: Lovisa's share price against its earnings per share for five years, and Woolworths's closing price against its earnings per share.
Compute P/E and read the change over time: price and profit moving in different directions.
Turn to cash: free cash flow for each company from the cash flow statement, after capital spending and lease principal, against profit and dividends.
Show the gap between book and market: equity per share against price, and ASIC's remark that market capitalisation is not a fair value.
Introduce discounted cash flow and enterprise value as the framework behind a price, with their sensitivity.
Close with what a price is a bet on, and what you would want to know.
examples: Woolworths: closing price $40.24 and basic EPS 93.2 cents give a P/E of about 43 on statutory earnings; before significant items EPS was 130.9 cents, a P/E of about 31.

Free cash flow after property, plant and equipment spending and lease principal: Woolworths about 1,215 ($M) against profit of 1,152 and dividends paid of 1,100; Lovisa about 85,134 ($000s) against profit of 95,590 and dividends of 88,589, with facility borrowings of 10,000.
Lovisa book value: 95,590 / 0.8632 gives about 110.7 million shares; equity of 77,961 per share is about $0.70, against a price of $23.25, about 33 times.

questionPlan.sample: Two analysts forecast the same cash flows for a company and use slightly different discount rates, and their values are far apart. Why?

choices: It removes cash from both companies, which makes the borrowed company look safer
It always gives a lower number than market capitalisation, so it is a more cautious measure of what a business is worth

courseCheck: A mixed set that puts a real company in front of the learner: tag lines of a balance sheet and trace a transaction through the equation; place a sale and a cost in the right period; reconcile profit to operating cash flow and say which line explains the gap; decide whether a net current liability is a warning, using the going concern note; read gearing with and without leases; say what a very high ROE hides; find a figure in the notes that the face of the statements blur; run an invented set of three years of figures through the warning-sign checks; and read a P/E and a free cash flow figure for what the price assumes.
platformNeeds: Numeric answers with a stated tolerance and rounding rule. Most numeric samples here are rounded readings ('to one decimal place', 'accept 30 to 32'), not exact sums.

Statement extracts that render as small tables with an attribution line. The pack's extracts are tables of figures from annual reports, and the `extracts` field is text. Fallback: a `table` figure above the question with the source named in the prompt.

A `statement_explorer` figure that shows one company's three statements side by side and highlights, when a line is tapped, where its twin appears (for example depreciation in profit and in the reconciliation). Fallback: the `table` and `svg_figure` pairs described in lessons 1 to 5.
A ratio worksheet figure where the learner fills in cells and the figure checks them within a rounding tolerance (lessons 8 to 11). Fallback: numeric questions.
unverified: Every figure of Woolworths, Lovisa, ASIC, IFRS and the textbook is in the pack. These are not: AASB numbers for IAS 2 and IAS 7 (AASB 102 and 107), which the planner wrote from memory and which no pack page states. Use 'IAS 2' and 'IAS 7' and say Australian companies apply them as AASB standards.
The reason for Lovisa's negative common control reserve of $208.9 million. The pack shows the figure on the balance sheet and nothing explains it. Say only that it sits in equity.

Lovisa's share count of about 110.7 million is the planner's own division of profit by basic EPS, not a figure from the report. Equity per share of $0.70 and the 33 times price to book follow from it.

The Lovisa return on capital of about 21% is the planner's arithmetic using Wikipedia's definition, the 28.7% tax rate (38,493 over 134,083) and a capital figure of equity, loans and lease liabilities less cash. It is a rough illustration and is not a figure the company reports.

That lease principal should be subtracted when comparing operating cash flow across companies, and that lease liabilities belong in gearing, are the planner's analytical judgements. The pack gives the facts (IFRS 16 puts leases on the balance sheet; principal is in financing) and not the instruction.
Centro: the pack gives one sentence ('billions of dollars of short-term debt', June 2011). It has no dollar figure, no account of the court's reasoning and nothing on dishonesty. Do not add any.
Slater and Gordon: the pack has ASIC's 2016 release only, with no loss figures, share price or dates beyond it.
Dick Smith: its Wikipedia article contains a claim about fraudulent accounting and a $125 million loan that is not backed by anything else in the pack. It is not used.

The invented cases (the joinery firm, Harbour Print, Dunmore Tiles, Alder Pty Ltd, the gym, the two retailers with a 20% ROE) are plainly invented and every figure in them was checked by the planner. Say so in the lessons.

Both annual reports are for the year to 28 June 2026 and were read from text extracted from PDFs. Tables can lose a column. Check each figure quoted in a lesson against the pack lines named in passages.md, not against memory.
